questions.stem: A researcher engineers a mutant strain of an enteric bacterium. The mutant still swims normally toward nutrients in soft agar but can no longer attach to cultured human intestinal epithelial cells. Loss of which structure most likely explains this defect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flagella

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nucleoid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Periplasmic space

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pili (fimbriae)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Porins

explanation.summary: Pili/fimbriae mediate adhesion; flagella mediate motility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pili, also called fimbriae, are tiny hair-like projections that carry adhesins (proteins or glycoproteins) allowing bacteria to attach to surfaces such as the human intestinal lining. Motility is preserved, so the flagella are intact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flagella provide whip-like motility and chemotaxis, which this mutant still has.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The nucleoid holds the circular chromosome and plays no direct role in attachment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The periplasmic space lies between the two membranes of gram-negatives and holds enzymes such as beta-lactamases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Porins are outer membrane protein channels that transport molecules, not attachment structures.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with a long-term urinary catheter develops fever, confusion, and a blood pressure of 78/40 mm Hg. Blood cultures grow organisms that appear pink on Gram stain. Which bacterial component most likely triggered his hypotension?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lipopolysaccharide of the outer membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mycolic acids of an acid-fast wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polysaccharide capsule around the wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sterols in the cytoplasmic membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teichoic acids of a thick cell wall

explanation.summary: Gram-negative LPS (endotoxin) causes septic shock.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pink organisms on Gram stain are gram-negative, and only gram-negatives carry lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in an outer membrane. LPS is an endotoxin that can drive sepsis, septic shock, and multiorgan failure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mycolic acids characterize acid-fast organisms such as Mycobacteria, which are Gram nonreactive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A capsule protects against phagocytosis; it is not the endotoxin that causes shock.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Membrane sterols are the notable exception of Mycoplasma and are not linked to septic shock.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Teichoic and lipoteichoic acids belong to gram-positive walls, which stain purple, not pink.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with gram-negative bacteremia becomes hypotensive and develops multiorgan failure. Endotoxin from her organism produces the fall in blood pressure chiefly through which mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A secreted paralytic toxin that acts on nerves and muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Germinating spores that physically block small blood vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolytic toxins that lyse red cells to harvest their iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron-chelating compounds that strip iron from transferrin

choices.label: E
choices.text: TLR signaling causing cytokine release and vasodilation

explanation.summary: LPS acts through toll-like receptors, triggering cytokine-driven vasodilation and leak.
explanation.whyCorrect: LPS interacts with toll-like receptors on immune cells, causing release of cytokines and other inflammatory factors. These dilate blood vessels and increase their permeability, lowering blood pressure and organ blood flow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A secreted paralytic toxin is an exotoxin, as with botulinum toxin; endotoxin is a structural component.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Spores are dormant survival structures and do not cause shock by blocking vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemolysins help bacteria obtain iron; they are not how endotoxin causes shock.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chelators steal iron from host proteins; they do not cause vasodilation.

questions.stem: A laboratory technician floods a smear with crystal violet, then iodide, and then a decolorizing agent. One organism remains deep purple after decolorization, while another has lost its color. Which feature of the purple organism explains its retention of the dye?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A cell wall rich in mycolic acids

choices.label: B
choices.text: A polysaccharide capsule layer

choices.label: C
choices.text: A thick peptidoglycan cell wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: An outer membrane containing porins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sterols within the cytoplasmic membrane

explanation.summary: Thick peptidoglycan retains the crystal violet-iodide complex in gram-positives.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gram-positive bacteria have thick peptidoglycan walls that hold the crystal violet-iodide complex after decolorization, so they appear deep purple or blue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mycolic acid-rich (atypical) bacteria are Gram nonreactive and are identified by acid-fast staining.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Capsules do not bind most dyes and are not why gram-positives stay purple.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An outer membrane with porins is a gram-negative feature; these cells lose the violet dye and take up safranin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Membrane sterols are a Mycoplasma exception and do not determine Gram reaction.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has had a productive cough for several months. His sputum smear is stained with carbol fuchsin and then washed with a decolorizer; slender red rods stand out against a blue counterstained background. Which property of these rods allows them to keep the red dye?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A polysaccharide capsule that excludes the dye

choices.label: B
choices.text: A thick peptidoglycan layer with teichoic acids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Abundant porins in the outer membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Large amounts of mycolic acids in the wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lipopolysaccharide within an outer membrane

explanation.summary: Mycolic acids make Mycobacteria and Nocardia acid-fast.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acid-fast bacteria such as Mycobacteria have large amounts of mycolic acids in their cell walls that resist decolorization by acid alcohol, so they stay bright red while the background takes up methylene blue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Capsules do not bind most dyes; they appear as clear halos with India ink.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thick peptidoglycan explains Gram-positive crystal violet retention, not resistance to acid alcohol.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Porins are transport channels and do not retain carbol fuchsin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: LPS is a gram-negative endotoxin and does not confer acid-fastness.

questions.stem: A bacterium recovered from a deep wound grows only in an oxygen-free culture chamber and dies quickly when exposed to room air. The patient is treated with metronidazole, a drug that exploits this organism's metabolism. Which deficiency accounts for the organism's sensitivity to air?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lack of enzymes for anaerobic fermentation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lack of porins and lipopolysaccharide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lack of secreted iron-chelating compounds

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lack of sterols in the cytoplasmic membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lack of superoxide dismutase and catalase

explanation.summary: Obligate anaerobes lack superoxide dismutase and catalase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Obligate anaerobes cannot live in an oxygen atmosphere because they lack superoxide dismutase and catalase, the enzymes that protect against oxygen free radicals. Metronidazole exploits this metabolic weakness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An organism lacking fermentation would fail without oxygen, the opposite of this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Porins and LPS are outer membrane parts of gram-negatives and are unrelated to oxygen tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chelators help pathogens obtain scarce iron; they do not protect against oxygen radicals.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Almost all bacteria lack membrane sterols, including aerobes, so this cannot explain oxygen toxicity.

questions.stem: Bacteria are inoculated into fresh broth. After an initial slow period, the population climbs so that the number of new cells formed at any moment is proportional to the number already present. This continues until space or nutrients run out. Which growth phase is described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Death phase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dormant phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exponential phase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lag phase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stationary phase

explanation.summary: Exponential (log) phase: growth proportional to population size.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the exponential (log) phase, growth is rapid and new cell production is proportional to the current population (1, 2, 4, 8...). It continues until resources such as space or nutrients are exhausted.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The death phase is a decline in the population.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dormancy with low CFUs describes the middle of a chronic infection, not rapid proportional growth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lag phase is the initial slow period when bacteria mature and adapt.
whyWrongByChoice.E: In the stationary phase new cells and dying cells roughly balance, so total count plateaus.

questions.stem: Two patients have bacterial infections. Patient 1, a 19-year-old, has fever, headache, and neck stiffness that worsened over less than 2 days; CSF shows gram-negative diplococci. Patient 2 has a cough that developed slowly over months; sputum shows acid-fast organisms. Which property best explains the difference in the tempo of their illnesses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Organism 1 divides about daily; organism 2 about hourly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Organism 1 divides about hourly; organism 2 about daily

choices.label: C
choices.text: Organism 1 has a mycolic wall; organism 2 a thin wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Organism 1 lacks a cell wall; organism 2 has a thick one

choices.label: E
choices.text: Organism 1 uses binary fission; organism 2 sporulation

explanation.summary: Division rate drives tempo: N. meningitidis about hourly vs M. tuberculosis about every 24 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neisseria meningitidis divides at least once per hour, so a few bacteria rapidly produce an invasive infection after a short prodrome. Mycobacterium tuberculosis divides about every 24 hours, so illness is chronic and slow to manifest.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the rates; the meningococcus is the fast divider.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycolic acids belong to the acid-fast organism, not to the gram-negative diplococci.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gram-negative diplococci have a thin peptidoglycan wall between two membranes; they do not lack a wall.
whyWrongByChoice.E: All clinically important bacteria discussed replicate by binary fission.

questions.stem: A Gram stain of pus from a skin abscess shows purple spherical cells bunched together like grapes. Which genus is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Escherichia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neisseria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nocardia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Staphylococcus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus

explanation.summary: Gram-positive cocci in clusters = Staphylococcus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gram-positive (purple) cocci arranged in grape-like clusters are characteristic of Staphylococcus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escherichia coli is a gram-negative organism and would stain pink.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neisseria forms gram-negative (pink) diplococci, in pairs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nocardia forms long thread-like filaments (hyphae) and is Gram nonreactive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Streptococcus forms gram-positive cocci in short single-file chains.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy is brought in because he has not stooled for several days. Over the next day he drools excessively, has little facial expression, and becomes weak. His parents had been dipping his pacifier in honey. What is the pathogenesis of his illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capsule blocking phagocytes in the infant's blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endotoxin released from gram-negative rods in the gut

choices.label: C
choices.text: Flagellated bacteria swimming into the spinal cord

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ingested spores germinated in the gut and made toxin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pili attaching bacteria directly to muscle fibers

explanation.summary: Infant botulism: honey-borne spores germinate in the immature gut and produce paralytic toxin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clostridium botulinum spores can contaminate honey. An infant's immature gut cannot clear them, so they germinate into toxin-forming bacteria, and the paralytic toxin causes constipation, drooling, facial weakness, and muscle weakness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A capsule helps evade phagocytosis but does not explain toxin-mediated paralysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: LPS endotoxin causes sepsis and shock, not descending paralysis with constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The illness results from toxin produced in the gut, not bacterial invasion of nerve tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pili mediate adhesion; the paralysis here is caused by a toxin.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has a urinary tract infection caused by a gram-negative rod that fails to respond to a beta-lactam antibiotic. Testing shows the isolate produces an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL). Where is this enzyme located, and how does it confer resistance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the capsule, trapping the drug in polysaccharide

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the cytoplasm, altering the ribosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the nucleoid, rewriting penicillin-binding proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the outer membrane, closing its porin channels

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the periplasmic space, cleaving the drug's ring

explanation.summary: Gram-negative beta-lactamases act in the periplasmic space by hydrolyzing the beta-lactam ring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gram-negative beta-lactamases such as ESBLs, AmpC, and carbapenemases sit in the periplasmic space between the inner and outer membranes and hydrolyze the beta-lactam ring, so the drug cannot bind penicillin-binding proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Capsules protect against phagocytosis; they are not the location of beta-lactamases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ribosomes carry out translation and are not the target of beta-lactams or beta-lactamases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-lactamases act on the drug itself in the periplasm, not within the nucleoid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Porins are outer membrane transport channels; beta-lactamases are periplasmic enzymes that destroy the drug.

questions.stem: Tears and saliva contain an enzyme that helps protect the eyes and mouth from bacteria and is especially effective against gram-positive organisms. Which action of this enzyme, and which reason for its gram-positive preference, are correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Breaks peptide cross-links within the periplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleaves NAG-NAM bonds in an exposed wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degrades sterols in the cytoplasmic membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dissolves mycolic acids in a waxy acid-fast wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hydrolyzes lipid A in an exposed outer membrane

explanation.summary: Lysozyme cleaves NAG-NAM beta-1,4 bonds; gram-positive walls are exposed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lysozyme breaks the beta-1,4 linkages between NAG and NAM, weakening peptidoglycan and causing lysis. It works especially well on gram-positives because their cell wall is more exposed, with no outer membrane covering it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gram-positives lack a periplasmic space, and lysozyme acts on the NAG-NAM glycosidic bonds.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Most bacterial membranes lack sterols, and lysozyme targets peptidoglycan.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mycolic acids belong to acid-fast organisms, not to typical gram-positives.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gram-positives have no outer membrane or lipid A; LPS is exclusive to gram-negatives.

questions.stem: A microbiologist grows an ampicillin-resistant E. coli strain together with a susceptible strain. Resistance spreads to the susceptible strain only when the cells are allowed to touch; separating the strains with a filter that passes free DNA and viruses but not cells prevents the spread. Which process best accounts for the transfer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binary fission

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conjugation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Generalized transduction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specialized transduction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transformation

explanation.summary: Conjugation transfers plasmids from one bacterium to another through direct physical contact.
explanation.whyCorrect: Conjugation requires a sex pilus from an F+ donor to attach to an F- recipient and form a mating bridge, so the cells must touch. A filter that blocks cells but passes DNA and phages abolishes only this mechanism. The transferred plasmids usually carry antibiotic resistance genes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binary fission produces clones of one cell and does not move genes between strains.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A phage vector could cross the filter, so phage-mediated transfer would not be blocked.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Temperate phages could also cross the filter; this mechanism needs no cell contact.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uptake of naked DNA would still occur across a filter that lets free DNA pass.

questions.stem: Heat-killed, lysed Streptococcus pneumoniae carrying a resistance marker are mixed with live susceptible S. pneumoniae. Live cells soon acquire the marker. Adding an enzyme that degrades free DNA to the medium completely prevents this, while blocking cell contact and removing phages do not. Which process is responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjugation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Generalized transduction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Site-specific recombination of the F plasmid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specialized transduction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transformation

explanation.summary: Transformation is uptake of naked DNA from the environment by a competent bacterium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The DNA comes from dying or lysed cells and is taken up directly by competent bacteria such as S. pneumoniae, so destroying free DNA stops it. The absorbed DNA is integrated into the chromosome by homologous recombination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjugation needs a mating bridge between living cells; blocking contact did not stop transfer here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Packaging of host DNA in a phage coat also depends on phages, which were removed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Integration of the F plasmid creates Hfr strains for conjugation, not uptake of free DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phage-mediated transfer protects DNA inside a capsid and was excluded by removing phages.

questions.stem: During lytic growth of a phage in a bacterial culture, a few new phage particles contain randomly chosen fragments of host bacterial DNA instead of viral DNA. These particles then deliver the bacterial DNA into new host cells. Which process is described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: F+ x F- conjugation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Generalized transduction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hfr conjugation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specialized transduction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transformation

explanation.summary: Generalized transduction is a packaging process in which lytic phages mispackage random host DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: In generalized transduction, some phages produced during lytic growth are packaged with host bacterial DNA rather than viral DNA; these transducing phages carry random donor DNA into a new cell, where it is swapped into the chromosome by homologous recombination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Plasmid transfer through a sex pilus does not involve phage particles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transfer from a chromosome with an integrated F plasmid happens across a mating bridge, not inside phages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Specialized transduction is an excision process that carries only DNA adjacent to an integrated prophage, not random fragments.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uptake of naked DNA needs no phage vector.

questions.stem: A nontoxigenic strain of Corynebacterium diphtheriae becomes toxin-producing after it is infected by a bacteriophage that does not lyse it. The new trait is passed to all daughter cells. Which event best explains how this strain acquired the toxin gene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Integration of temperate phage DNA into the chromosome as a prophage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Random host DNA packaged into a lytic phage capsid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spontaneous point mutation during DNA polymerase III replication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transfer of an F plasmid through a mating bridge

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uptake of naked DNA released from lysed toxigenic cells

explanation.summary: Temperate phages integrate as prophages and often encode bacterial toxins such as diphtheria toxin.
explanation.whyCorrect: A temperate bacteriophage injects viral DNA that incorporates into the host genome as a dormant prophage, which does not cause lysis and is passed to child cells. Temperate phages often carry genes for virulence proteins, with diphtheria, cholera, botulinum, Shiga-like and erythrogenic toxins as prime examples.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A transducing phage from generalized transduction carries random bacterial DNA, not the phage-borne toxin gene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A spontaneous mutation would not follow phage infection or create a toxin gene de novo in this way.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Conjugation requires a sex pilus and mating bridge, not a phage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transformation involves free DNA, not infection by a phage.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man who recently hiked in a wooded area develops an expanding red skin lesion and is diagnosed with Lyme disease. He is started on doxycycline. Which bacterial structure does this drug target to stop protein production?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 30S small ribosomal subunit

choices.label: B
choices.text: 40S small ribosomal subunit

choices.label: C
choices.text: 50S large ribosomal subunit

choices.label: D
choices.text: 60S large ribosomal subunit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Penicillin-binding proteins of the wall

explanation.summary: Tetracyclines such as doxycycline target the 30S subunit of the bacterial 70S ribosome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, composed of a 50S large and a 30S small subunit, and they differ from human 80S ribosomes, which makes them antibiotic targets. Doxycycline binds the 30S subunit and prevents bacterial protein production; it is commonly used for zoonotic infections such as Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The 40S is the small subunit of human 80S ribosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The 50S is the bacterial large subunit, but tetracyclines act on the small subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The 60S is the large subunit of human 80S ribosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillin-binding proteins are the target of beta-lactams, which block peptidoglycan cross-linking.

questions.stem: An E. coli isolate carries a beta-lactamase gene on its chromosome. After several generations, the same gene is found on a plasmid in the same cell and can then be shared with other bacteria. Which genetic element most directly allowed the gene to move from the chromosome onto the plasmid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacteriophage capsid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competence factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Origin of replication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sex pilus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transposon

explanation.summary: Transposons let DNA sequences jump within a genome, including between chromosome and plasmids.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transposons contain enzyme-coding genes that allow transposition of DNA sequences, moving them around the genome and between chromosomal and plasmid DNA, often carrying drug resistance genes. Once on a plasmid, the beta-lactamase gene can be transferred to other bacteria by conjugation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The capsid is the protein coat of a phage and stays outside the infected cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Competence describes the ability to take up naked DNA from the environment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The origin is where replication or plasmid transfer begins; it does not relocate genes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sex pilus forms the mating bridge for transfer between cells, not movement within one cell.

questions.stem: A researcher compares chromosome copying in E. coli with copying in human cells. Which feature is characteristic of the bacterial process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is slower because the genome is much longer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Replication occurs inside a membrane-bound nucleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: The products are two linear double-stranded chromosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unwinding begins at a single origin of replication

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unwinding proceeds without any helicase enzyme

explanation.summary: Bacterial replication begins at a single origin, whereas human DNA has multiple origins.
explanation.whyCorrect: A bacterial helicase unwinds the circular double-stranded chromosome starting at a single origin of replication, in contrast to the multiple origins on human DNA. DNA polymerase III then replicates and proofreads, yielding two identical circular chromosomes, and the shorter genome makes the process simpler and quicker.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The E. coli genome is far shorter than the human genome, and replication is quicker.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacteria are prokaryotes and have no nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The products are two circular double-stranded chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A bacterial helicase is required to unwind the strands.

questions.stem: In a mating experiment, a donor E. coli strain repeatedly passes segments of its chromosomal genes, not just plasmid genes, to F- recipients. Which property of the donor best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It carries a free F plasmid in its cytoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: It contains transposons flanking each chromosomal gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: It harbors a temperate phage that is imprecisely excised

choices.label: D
choices.text: It releases naked chromosomal DNA that recipients absorb

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its F plasmid has been integrated into the chromosome

explanation.summary: Hfr strains carry the F plasmid integrated into the chromosome and can transfer flanking chromosomal DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: In high-frequency recombination (Hfr) strains, the F plasmid is integrated into the chromosome by site-specific recombination. Transfer starts at the origin within the F sequence, so flanking chromosomal DNA can follow, usually only a fragment of the donor chromosome. In ordinary F+ x F- mating, there is no transfer of chromosomal DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A free F plasmid in an F+ donor is transferred without chromosomal DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transposons move sequences within a genome; they do not make conjugation carry chromosomal genes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imprecise excision of a prophage is specialized transduction, a phage process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Release and uptake of free DNA is transformation and does not require mating with F- cells.

questions.stem: An Hfr donor is mixed with an F- recipient, and mating pairs are sheared apart in a blender after only a few minutes, breaking the mating bridge. Which donor genes are most likely to have entered the recipient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A random selection of genes from across the chromosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genes located closest to the origin of transfer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genes located farthest from the origin of transfer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only the genes encoding the sex pilus

choices.label: E
choices.text: The complete donor chromosome

explanation.summary: Interrupted conjugation transfers only the genes nearest the origin of transfer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hfr transfer begins at the origin in the integrated F plasmid sequence and proceeds linearly. If the mating bridge breaks early, the recipient receives only part of the donor DNA, namely the genes closest to the origin. Timing the interruption in this way is useful for mapping gene order experimentally.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjugal transfer is ordered from the origin, not random; random fragments fit generalized transduction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Distant genes enter last and are the first to be lost when mating is interrupted.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transfer begins at the origin within the F sequence; it is not limited to pilus genes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Even uninterrupted Hfr transfer usually passes only a fragment of the donor chromosome.

questions.stem: A single E. coli cell lands on a catheter surface and within hours establishes a large colony of genetically identical cells. Which process produced this colony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binary fission producing two clones per cycle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Budding of daughter cells from a parent spore

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lysogeny of the cell by a temperate phage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mating of two cells that mix their chromosomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeated uptake of DNA from neighboring cells

explanation.summary: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission, yielding two clones and doubling the population each cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacteria are haploid and undergo clonal division rather than sexual reproduction. Each binary fission produces two clones of the same cell, so the population doubles every cycle, which makes colonization and invasion easy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The lecture describes bacterial reproduction as division into two clones, not budding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A prophage becomes dormant within a cell; it does not generate the colony.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bacteria do not reproduce by mixing chromosomes from two parents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uptake of free DNA is transformation, a gene-exchange mechanism, not reproduction.

questions.stem: A patient with an E. coli infection is treated with amoxicillin but does not improve. The isolate produces an enzyme that destroys the drug before it can reach its target. What does this enzyme do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alters the sex pilus receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocks entry of the drug through porins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degrades beta-lactam antibiotics

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methylates the 30S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pumps tetracyclines out of the cell

explanation.summary: Beta-lactamase is an enzyme that degrades beta-lactam antibiotics and provides resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ampicillin, amoxicillin and piperacillin are beta-lactams that bind penicillin-binding proteins and prevent cross-linking of the peptidoglycan cell wall. A cell carrying a beta-lactamase gene degrades these drugs, and the gene can spread on plasmids to other bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The sex pilus mediates conjugation and is unrelated to amoxicillin action.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced entry does not destroy the drug, which is what the stem describes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amoxicillin acts on penicillin-binding proteins, not the 30S subunit; the stem describes drug destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Efflux of tetracyclines would not explain amoxicillin failure, and efflux does not destroy the drug.

questions.stem: An F+ E. coli cell forms a mating bridge with an F- cell. Which describes the DNA that crosses the bridge and what happens next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A random chromosome fragment crosses and recombines homologously

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both plasmid strands cross and the donor loses its plasmid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both plasmid strands cross, along with a large chromosome segment

choices.label: D
choices.text: One chromosome strand crosses, starting at the chromosomal origin

choices.label: E
choices.text: One plasmid strand crosses, and each cell then synthesizes its complement

explanation.summary: In F+ x F- conjugation, one strand of the F plasmid crosses and both cells restore the double strand.
explanation.whyCorrect: A single strand of the double-stranded F plasmid is transferred across the mating bridge, starting at the origin of the plasmid, and no chromosomal DNA is transferred. Each bacterium then synthesizes the complementary strand, restoring a double-stranded plasmid in both cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Random chromosomal fragments recombining homologously fits generalized transduction or transformation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Only one strand is transferred, and the donor retains a complete double-stranded plasmid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only a single plasmid strand crosses, and F+ x F- mating transfers no chromosomal DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chromosomal DNA is not transferred in F+ x F- mating; that occurs only in Hfr strains.

questions.stem: A researcher quantifies resident microbes in samples taken from several body sites of a healthy adult. Which site is expected to harbor the greatest number of microbes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dental plaque

choices.label: C
choices.text: Skin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stomach

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vagina

explanation.summary: The colon carries by far the most normal flora, about 10^14 microbes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microbe concentration rises steeply as one descends the GI tract, and the colon holds the highest concentration of normal flora, about 10^14 organisms. These are mostly anaerobes such as Bacteroides species.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dental plaque is dense (about 10^12) but still about 100-fold below the large bowel.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Skin carries about 10^11 microbes, far fewer than the large bowel.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastric acidity limits growth; the stomach holds only about 10^7 microbes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vagina holds roughly 10^7 to 10^8 microbes.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman develops cramping, abdominal tenderness, and watery diarrhea 12 times a day after 2 weeks of broad-spectrum antibiotics for pneumonia. Colonoscopy shows yellow-white membranous plaques adherent to the mucosa. Which of the following best explains how her illness arose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct toxicity of the antibiotic to the colonic epithelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ingestion of a preformed toxin in contaminated food

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invasion of the colonic wall by an inhaled respiratory pathogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overgrowth of a resident gut organism after loss of competing flora

choices.label: E
choices.text: Translocation of colonic bacteria into the peritoneal cavity

explanation.summary: Antibiotics kill competing gut flora, letting resident C. difficile overgrow and cause pseudomembranous colitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. difficile is normal flora of the lower GI tract, normally held in check by other flora competing for space and food. Antibiotics remove that competition, so C. difficile overgrows and its toxins damage the lining, producing yellow-white pseudomembranes and watery diarrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The antibiotic acts indirectly by killing competing flora; bacterial toxins damage the lining.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The organism involved is already a member of lower GI flora; this is not a food-borne intoxication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The disease arises from the patient's own gut flora, not from spread of her pneumonia pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spillage into the peritoneum causes peritonitis, not mucosal pseudomembranes.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman who douches regularly reports a thin, grayish discharge with a strong fishy odor. She has little itching or pain. Pelvic examination shows the walls coated with thin gray discharge and minimal inflammation. Overgrowth of which organism is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gardnerella vaginalis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lactobacillus species

choices.label: D
choices.text: Staphylococcus saprophyticus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Bacterial vaginosis is usually caused by overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacterial vaginosis presents with a thin white or grayish discharge with a fishy smell from released amines, minimal inflammation, and little pain. Douching is a common risk factor, and the usual cause is overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida causes thick white discharge with intense itching and inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactobacillus is the protective dominant flora that keeps the pH near 4.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. saprophyticus is a urinary tract pathogen, not a cause of this discharge.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is nasopharyngeal flora associated with otitis media.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: In healthy premenopausal women, a dominant resident organism ferments glycogen from the epithelium of the lower genital tract, keeping the pH near 4 and inhibiting pathogens. Which organism is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enterococcus species

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gardnerella vaginalis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lactobacillus species

choices.label: E
choices.text: Staphylococcus epidermidis

explanation.summary: Lactobacillus species make lactic acid from glycogen, giving the vagina a pH of about 4.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lactobacillus species are the dominant vaginal flora. They ferment glycogen into lactic acid, lowering the pH to about 4, which inhibits pathogenic microbes and prevents overgrowth of other normal flora.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida is a yeast that overgrows when the protective flora are disrupted.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enterococcus is present in small numbers but is not the acid producer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gardnerella is present in some women but causes bacterial vaginosis when it overgrows.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. epidermidis is present but does not set the acidic pH.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy has ear pain and a moderate fever after a cold. Otoscopy shows a red, inflamed eardrum with pus behind it. His father asks why young children have these infections far more often than adults. Which anatomic feature best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A longer, wider, more vertical Eustachian tube

choices.label: B
choices.text: A shorter, narrower, more horizontal Eustachian tube

choices.label: C
choices.text: A sterile external canal that lacks skin flora

choices.label: D
choices.text: Absence of any flora in the young nasopharynx

choices.label: E
choices.text: Persistence of maternal IgG through the second year

explanation.summary: Children's short, narrow, horizontal Eustachian tubes impair drainage and let nasopharyngeal flora reach the middle ear.
explanation.whyCorrect: The short, narrow, more horizontal Eustachian tube in children makes middle-ear drainage harder and makes it easier for nasopharyngeal flora to migrate in. Its small diameter also blocks easily with inflammation or mucus from upper respiratory infections or allergies, trapping bacteria that proliferate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This describes the adult orientation, which drains the middle ear more easily.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infection comes from nasopharyngeal flora reaching the middle ear, not the external canal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Children carry nasopharyngeal flora; those flora are the source of the infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transplacental IgG wanes by 3-6 months and does not explain the anatomy.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 5-month-old unvaccinated infant whose parents declined all immunizations develops severe invasive pneumococcal disease after starting daycare. He was well during his first months of life despite household exposure to colds. Which change best explains his new susceptibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquisition of only unencapsulated pneumococcal strains

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of oligosaccharides after weaning from breastmilk

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maturation of Peyer patches that suppresses immunity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replacement of birth-canal Lactobacillus by skin flora

choices.label: E
choices.text: Waning of maternal IgG acquired across the placenta

explanation.summary: Transplacental IgG wanes 3-6 months after birth, opening a window of susceptibility that vaccines at 2 months are meant to close.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maternal IgG crossing the placenta protects the infant early, but titers fall 3-6 months after birth, before the infant makes adequate antibodies of his own. Exposure to S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, or N. meningitidis in that window can cause severe infection, which is why Hib and pneumococcal vaccines begin at 2 months.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Unencapsulated strains are much less likely to cause invasive disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Breastmilk oligosaccharides are prebiotics for the microbiota, not antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gut lymphoid development supports, rather than suppresses, immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shifts in early flora do not explain loss of antibody protection.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: An enteric pathogen ingested by a healthy adult survives gastric acid but fails to establish itself in the intestine. Apart from competing for space and nutrients, the resident flora most directly impede it by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Breaking down IgA and mucus in the intestinal lining

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutralizing gastric acid before it reaches the duodenum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Producing vitamin K that lyses bacterial cell walls

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raising the luminal oxygen level to block anaerobes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secreting acids, proteins, and fatty acids that inhibit growth

explanation.summary: Colonization resistance includes direct antimicrobial products from gut flora: acids, proteins, and fatty acids.
explanation.whyCorrect: Colonization resistance is the microbiome's prevention of pathogen colonization. Beyond occupying space and consuming food, GI flora produce acids, proteins, and fatty acids that directly impede the growth of other bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Flora stimulate, rather than degrade, IgA and mucus production.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutralizing acid would help, not hinder, ingested microbes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Colonic vitamin K serves host metabolism; it is not antibacterial.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gut flora are mostly anaerobes themselves; they do not raise oxygen.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a white plaque coating his tongue and buccal mucosa. He has taken no antibiotics or hormones, has had no oral trauma, and has natural teeth. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics

choices.label: B
choices.text: Obtain a complete blood count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reassure him that this resolves without evaluation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Refit his dentures to improve the oral seal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Send stool for clostridial toxin testing

explanation.summary: Thrush with no obvious trigger should prompt a check of the immune system (CBC).
explanation.whyCorrect: Thrush is Candida overgrowth in the mouth, usually triggered by antibiotics, birth control, trauma, poorly fitting dentures, or immunosuppression. When no obvious cause is present, check the immune system with a CBC, because opportunistic infections can be a sign of immune failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics kill bacteria and are themselves a trigger for Candida overgrowth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Unexplained oral candidiasis can signal a failing immune system and warrants evaluation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: He has natural teeth, so poorly fitting dentures are not the cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stool toxin testing addresses C. difficile colitis, not oral plaques.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman develops intense vulvar itching, redness, swelling, and a thick white discharge one week after finishing amoxicillin for sinusitis. White plaques are seen on the inflamed mucosa. Which mechanism best explains how her medication led to this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It eliminated Gardnerella, allowing Lactobacillus to overgrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: It killed commensal bacteria, freeing resources for a resident yeast

choices.label: C
choices.text: It made the sexual acquisition of a foreign fungus more likely

choices.label: D
choices.text: It raised estrogen, increasing glycogen for a resident yeast

choices.label: E
choices.text: It selected a resistant bacterium that now invades the mucosa

explanation.summary: Antibiotics cause dysbiosis by killing commensal bacteria, letting Candida albicans overgrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Candida albicans is normal flora of the oral, GI, and vaginal tracts. Antibiotics kill both pathogenic and commensal bacteria, increasing resources available to Candida, which becomes dominant and causes vulvovaginal candidiasis with itching, erythema, thick white discharge, and white plaque.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactobacillus is protective; its loss, not its overgrowth, promotes infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Candida albicans is already part of normal flora; it was not newly acquired.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amoxicillin does not raise estrogen; its effect is on bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thick white discharge and plaques point to a fungal, not bacterial, cause.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 61-year-old postmenopausal woman has a vaginal pH of 5, compared with a pH of 4 measured during her reproductive years. Compared with that earlier value, the hydrogen ion concentration of her vaginal fluid is now approximately which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Essentially unchanged

choices.label: B
choices.text: One-half as high

choices.label: C
choices.text: One-tenth as high

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ten times as high

choices.label: E
choices.text: Twice as high

explanation.summary: Falling estrogen raises vaginal pH from 4 toward 5, a 10-fold drop in hydrogen ions that favors overgrowth and infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Estrogen promotes glycogen release from vaginal epithelium, fueling lactic acid production by Lactobacillus. As estrogen declines with age, the pH approaches 5. Because pH is logarithmic, a shift from 4 to 5 is a 10-fold decrease in hydrogen ion concentration, raising the risk of overgrowth and infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A full unit of pH change is a large, 10-fold change.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The pH scale is logarithmic; one unit is a 10-fold change, not 2-fold.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A higher pH means fewer hydrogen ions, not more.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A rise in pH reflects a fall in hydrogen ions, and the scale is logarithmic.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 22-year-old sexually active woman has dysuria and urinary frequency. Her urine culture grows an organism that is normal flora of the gastrointestinal tract and vagina and that is second only to Escherichia coli as a cause of urinary tract infections. Which organism is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enterococcus species

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gardnerella vaginalis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Staphylococcus epidermidis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Staphylococcus saprophyticus

explanation.summary: S. saprophyticus, GI and vaginal flora, is the second most common cause of UTI after E. coli.
explanation.whyCorrect: S. saprophyticus is normal flora of the gastrointestinal tract and vagina and is the second most common cause of urinary tract infections. Only E. coli, also GI flora, causes more UTIs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterococcus is gut flora but is not identified as the second most common UTI cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gardnerella causes bacterial vaginosis, not urinary tract infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: S. aureus causes skin infections, pneumonia, and sepsis; it is not the second most common uropathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. epidermidis is skin flora and is not cited as a leading UTI cause.

questions.topicName: Normal Flora: Role in Health and Disease

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has had four episodes of Clostridioides difficile colitis. Each responds to antibiotics, but symptoms return soon after therapy stops, and she has lost 40 pounds. Which intervention after her current antibiotic course is most likely to prevent another recurrence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A longer course of the same antibiotic regimen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Instillation of screened donor stool by colonoscopy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Instillation of unscreened stool from a relative

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switching to a different broad-spectrum antibiotic

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaginal Lactobacillus therapy to restore acidity

explanation.summary: Fecal microbiota transplantation quickly reestablishes gut flora and cures about 91-93% of recurrent C. difficile.
explanation.whyCorrect: Repeated antibiotics kill normal flora trying to reestablish their niche, so recurrence rates are high. A fecal transplant, in which screened donor stool is liquefied in saline and usually given by colonoscopy, rapidly restores normal flora; about 91-93% of patients recover without further recurrence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The antibiotics that kill C. difficile also kill reestablishing flora, perpetuating recurrence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor stool must be screened so dangerous microbes are not introduced.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Any broad-spectrum agent further depletes flora and sets up reinfection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaginal flora do not restore the colonic microbiota.
